rules.heading: Language segmentation
points: Belgium requires two distinct versions: Dutch (Flemish) for Flanders and French for Wallonia. Brussels is bilingual—default to dual-language assets or choose based on media buy.
Luxembourg prefers French and German; Luxembourgish is a bonus but not required. English is widely accepted in advertising due to high foreign-born population.
Netherlands uses Dutch but is highly English-proficient. English can work for global brands, but Dutch localizations perform better for emotional resonance.
France requires formal, polished French; informal registers are risky outside youth or digital-native contexts.

rules.heading: Tone and register
points: Belgians are more reserved, formal, and indirect than the Dutch. Use a more formal register in Dutch campaigns for Belgium than you would in the Netherlands.
French Belgians and French audiences expect formal address (vous) in most advertising contexts. Informal (tu) may work in youth/social media but requires careful judgment.
Flemish audiences interact more with content (polls, shares, stories); French-speaking audiences are less engaged with interactive formats.

rules.heading: Cultural values
points: Emphasize quality, craftsmanship, and heritage. Overt hard-sell tactics feel pushy; understatement and sophistication resonate.
Relationship-building matters in Wallonia and France; Flemish audiences are more receptive to direct product benefit messaging.
Avoid using "Franglais" excessively in France; it is more accepted among young, urban Belgians but can alienate older or rural French audiences.

rules.heading: Regulatory and practical
points: French language laws (Toubon Law) may require French-language versions of all claims and supers for France-market assets.
Ensure all legal and disclaimer copy is adapted to local requirements per country (France, Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg each have distinct consumer protection norms).

rules.heading: Communication style
points: Modesty is essential. Avoid overt boasting about product superiority or aggressive comparative claims. Japanese advertising rarely directly criticizes competitors.
Indirect, suggestive storytelling is preferred over explicit benefit claims. Let viewers infer value rather than being told.
Use the celebrity halo effect—celebrities endorse products without detailed benefit explanations. The celebrity's credibility transfers to the brand implicitly.

rules.heading: Kawaii and mascots
points: Cute characters, mascots, and anime-style illustrations are widely accepted and expected in many categories, even for adult audiences. They serve as trusted "messengers" for the brand.
"Kawaii" is nuanced: it includes imperfection, expressionlessness, and healing qualities—not just Western-style cuteness. Characters like Hello Kitty resonate because they allow emotional projection.

rules.heading: Visual and aesthetic norms
points: Softer color palettes, minimalism, and nature imagery are common. Avoid aggressive, high-contrast Western ad aesthetics unless targeting a specific subculture.
Respect for traditional crafts is paramount. Do not depict traditional items (kimono, obi, tea ceremony objects) being misused or disrespected—this can cause brand damage.

rules.heading: Regulatory and social
points: Stealth marketing is heavily criticized and self-regulated by JARO (Japan Advertising Review Organization). Influencer and native ads must be clearly disclosed.
Superlatives are restricted. Claims like "No. 1" or "best" require substantiation under the Act Against Unjustifiable Premiums and Misleading Representations.
Avoid sexualized imagery. While legal boundaries may be broader, such content increasingly faces public criticism and withdrawal pressure.

rules.heading: Language
points: Use Japanese. English words may be sprinkled for style (loan words are common) but core messaging must be in natural Japanese.
Honorific language (keigo) is expected in formal or corporate contexts.

rules.heading: Hierarchy and respect
points: Age and seniority are central to Korean social structure. Depict respectful relationships between generations; avoid scenarios where younger people dismiss or disrespect elders.
Use appropriate speech levels in dialogue: jondaetmal (formal/polite) for authority figures, elders, or professional contexts; banmal (casual) only among peers or close friends.
Avoid the "kkondae" stereotype (rigid, condescending older person) or "ajumma" caricatures—these are derogatory and may alienate audiences.

rules.heading: Hallyu and modernity
points: Korean audiences are highly attuned to global trends but expect content that reflects Korean identity and pride. Hallyu (the Korean Wave) has elevated expectations for production quality and cultural authenticity.
K-pop and K-drama aesthetics (polished visuals, aspirational lifestyles, emotional storytelling) are benchmarks. Low-budget or dated creative will underperform.
Celebrity endorsements are powerful but must feel authentic. Koreans value idols who "grow" with their fans; perfection is expected but relatability matters.

rules.heading: Regulatory constraints
points: Cosmetics and health claims are tightly regulated by the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS). Avoid:
Medical endorsements ("doctor recommended," "hospital exclusive").
Anti-aging exaggerations ("reduces skin age by 10 years").
Pharmaceutical-style claims ("reduces inflammation," "skin regeneration").
Human-derived ingredient confusion (clarify plant- or milk-derived if using EXO, exosome, liposome references).
"Natural" and "organic" claims for cosmetics are being phased out; ensure compliance with current MFDS labeling rules.

rules.heading: Cultural values
points: Collectivism and group harmony are valued. Depict teamwork, family cohesion, and social belonging.
Education and achievement are highly prized. Aspirational messaging around success, improvement, and self-betterment resonates.
Food and dining are social rituals. Shared meals (Korean BBQ, fried chicken and beer, home-cooked dishes) signal warmth and togetherness.

rules.heading: Language
points: Use Korean. English words are common in youth and tech contexts but should not replace Korean for primary messaging.
Subtlety and understatement are appreciated; avoid overly aggressive or boastful copy.

rules.heading: Regulatory constraints
points: Political content is prohibited in advertising. Do not include any political views, party references, or ideological messaging.
Obscene or adult content is strictly forbidden and criminalized under Turkish law. Avoid even mildly suggestive imagery.

Covert/surreptitious advertising is banned. Any advertisement must be clearly identifiable as an ad. Stealth marketing, native ads disguised as editorial, or influencer posts without disclosure violate Turkish law.
Avoid content that could be seen as exploiting children, the elderly, or disabled persons.
Advertising must not distort or denigrate cultural, moral, or positive social behaviors.

rules.heading: Cultural values
points: Family, hospitality, and community are core values. Depict warm, multi-generational family settings where appropriate.
Respect for elders and authority figures is expected. Avoid generational conflict or disrespectful portrayals of older characters.
Modesty in dress and behavior is important. Even for fashion or beauty, avoid Western-style provocative imagery.

rules.heading: Religious and social sensitivity
points: Turkey is a secular state but predominantly Muslim. Avoid imagery that conflicts with Islamic norms (alcohol consumption shown positively, pork products, revealing clothing, religious symbols used casually).
Ramadan and Eid are significant; adapt timing and messaging around these periods if relevant.
Do not reference Atatürk, the Turkish flag, or national symbols in ways that could be seen as trivializing or disrespectful.

rules.heading: Language
points: Use Turkish throughout. English or mixed-language copy is acceptable for global brands targeting urban youth but should not replace Turkish for mass-market campaigns.
Formal, respectful tone is preferred in most contexts.

rules.heading: Language and acculturation
points: Segment by acculturation level: Hispanic-dominant (prefer Spanish), bicultural (comfortable in both), and US-dominant (prefer English). Adapt language choice accordingly—Spanglish may resonate with bicultural audiences but alienate Hispanic-dominant viewers.

Avoid one-size-fits-all Spanish translations. Dialects vary significantly: Mexican Spanish differs from Cuban, Puerto Rican, Central American, and South American Spanish. Use region-appropriate vocabulary, slang, and expressions.
Respect the "Spanglish" register when appropriate—it signals cultural fluency but only works for bicultural segments. For Hispanic-dominant audiences, maintain clean, idiomatic Spanish.

rules.heading: Cultural values
points: Familia is central. Multigenerational family depictions (grandparents, parents, children together) feel authentic. Isolated-individual narratives common in general-market US ads may feel cold or disconnected.
Emphasize community, tradition, and shared experiences—collective celebration over individual achievement.

Reference culturally meaningful moments: quinceañeras, Día de los Muertos, Fiestas Patrias, Carnaval, or regional traditions (Cuban coffee culture in Miami, Mexican breakfast rituals in Southern California).

rules.heading: Humor and tone
points: Humor often centers on family dynamics, cultural quirks, and shared generational experiences. Avoid sarcasm that could be misread or humor that plays on stereotypes.
Warm, emotionally resonant storytelling outperforms ironic or detached tones.

rules.heading: Representation
points: Cast talent that reflects the diversity within Hispanic communities (Afro-Latino, Indigenous, mixed heritage, range of skin tones). Avoid homogenizing "Hispanic" as a single look.
Do not exoticize or reduce culture to costumes, accents, or food alone—depict people in everyday, aspirational contexts.
